entries.meaning_short: A contract that lets software components request capabilities from another component or service.
entries.meaning_long: An API is the documented surface a program exposes so other software can call functions, exchange data, or automate a service without depending on implementation details.
examples: Use the GitHub REST API to list repository issues.

sources.title: API
sources.snippet: MDN defines API as a set of features and rules for interaction between software.

entries.meaning_short: A browser security mechanism for controlled cross-origin HTTP requests.
entries.meaning_long: CORS lets a server declare which origins may read selected responses in browsers, allowing cross-origin access without disabling the same-origin policy.
examples: Set Access-Control-Allow-Origin for a frontend hosted on a different domain.

sources.title: CORS
sources.snippet: MDN describes CORS as an HTTP-header mechanism for cross-origin resource access.

entries.meaning_short: The stylesheet language used to describe web page presentation.
entries.meaning_long: CSS controls visual styling such as layout, colors, typography, and responsive behavior for HTML and XML documents.
examples: Use CSS grid to lay out a dashboard.

sources.title: CSS
sources.snippet: MDN identifies CSS as the language for styling structured documents.

entries.meaning_short: A programming representation of a document tree.
entries.meaning_long: The DOM exposes document structure as objects and nodes that scripts can inspect and mutate at runtime.
examples: Query the DOM to update a button label after a click.

sources.title: DOM
sources.snippet: MDN presents the DOM as a document programming interface.

entries.meaning_short: The markup language used to structure web documents.
entries.meaning_long: HTML defines elements and document structure that browsers parse into the DOM and render as web pages.
examples: Use semantic HTML headings for accessible document structure.

sources.title: HTML
sources.snippet: MDN defines HTML as the standard markup language for web content structure.

entries.meaning_short: The application-layer protocol used for web resource transfer.
entries.meaning_long: HTTP defines request and response semantics that clients and servers use to exchange web resources, metadata, and status information.
examples: A browser sends an HTTP GET request for an HTML document.

sources.title: HTTP
sources.snippet: MDN documents HTTP as the protocol for fetching linked resources.

entries.meaning_short: HTTP carried over a secure transport layer.
entries.meaning_long: HTTPS protects HTTP traffic with TLS so clients can authenticate servers and encrypt data in transit.
examples: Serve login pages over HTTPS to protect credentials in transit.

sources.title: HTTPS
sources.snippet: MDN describes HTTPS as the secure version of HTTP.

entries.meaning_short: A text data format for structured values.
entries.meaning_long: JSON serializes objects, arrays, strings, numbers, booleans, and null in a compact text format used widely for APIs and configuration.
examples: Return JSON from a search API response.

sources.title: JSON
sources.snippet: MDN defines JSON as a standard text-based format for structured data.

entries.meaning_short: An architectural style for networked applications.
entries.meaning_long: REST describes constraints for resource-oriented systems, commonly implemented with HTTP methods, resource identifiers, stateless requests, and typed representations.
examples: Expose a REST endpoint that returns a project by id.

sources.title: REST
sources.snippet: MDN identifies REST as an architectural style for distributed hypermedia systems.

entries.meaning_short: A web app that updates one loaded page instead of navigating full documents.
entries.meaning_long: An SPA typically loads application code once and then changes views by fetching data and updating client-side state and DOM.
examples: A React dashboard can be built as an SPA.

sources.title: SPA
sources.snippet: MDN describes an SPA as a site that dynamically rewrites the current page.

entries.meaning_short: Rendering UI markup on the server before sending it to the client.
entries.meaning_long: SSR generates the initial HTML response on the server so users and crawlers can receive rendered content before client-side hydration or interactivity.
examples: Use SSR for a product page that needs fast first contentful paint.

sources.title: SSR
sources.snippet: MDN describes SSR as generating web pages on a server.

entries.meaning_short: A string that identifies a resource.
entries.meaning_long: A URI names or locates a resource using a standardized syntax; URLs are a common URI form that include location information.
examples: Use a URI to identify an API resource namespace.

sources.title: URI
sources.snippet: MDN defines URI as a string identifying a resource.

entries.meaning_short: A resource identifier that includes how and where to access a resource.
entries.meaning_long: A URL is a URI form that locates a resource, often including a scheme, host, path, query, and fragment.
examples: Copy the URL for a permanent entry detail page.

sources.title: URL
sources.snippet: MDN explains URL as the address of a unique resource on the Web.

entries.meaning_short: A web vulnerability where attacker-controlled script runs in another user's browser context.
entries.meaning_long: XSS occurs when untrusted data is rendered as executable script or markup, allowing attackers to steal data, act as users, or alter page behavior.
examples: Escape user comments before rendering them as HTML to prevent XSS.

sources.title: Cross-site scripting
sources.snippet: MDN documents cross-site scripting as client-side code injection.

entries.meaning_short: A compact token format for signed claims encoded as JSON.
entries.meaning_long: A JWT packages claims into a compact string that can be signed, and sometimes encrypted, for authentication and authorization flows.
examples: Send a JWT bearer token in an Authorization header.

sources.title: JSON Web Token
sources.snippet: Wikipedia describes JWT as a compact URL-safe token for JSON claims.

entries.meaning_short: A standard for identifying media formats and message parts.
entries.meaning_long: MIME types label content formats so clients can decide how to process responses, uploads, email parts, and embedded resources.
examples: Return application/json as the MIME type for a JSON API response.

sources.title: MIME type
sources.snippet: MDN explains MIME types as labels for file or byte-stream content formats.

entries.meaning_short: The distributed naming system that maps domain names to records such as IP addresses.
entries.meaning_long: DNS resolves human-readable domain names through a hierarchy of servers and record types used by browsers, services, and infrastructure.
examples: Create a DNS A record for a hosted web app.

sources.title: DNS
sources.snippet: MDN describes DNS as the system that maps domain names to IP addresses.

entries.meaning_short: A reliable transport protocol used by many network applications.
entries.meaning_long: TCP provides ordered, reliable byte-stream delivery between hosts and is commonly used beneath protocols such as HTTP and TLS.
examples: HTTP/1.1 commonly runs over a TCP connection.

sources.title: TCP
sources.snippet: MDN describes TCP as a transport-layer protocol for reliable delivery.

entries.meaning_short: A cryptographic protocol for securing network communication.
entries.meaning_long: TLS authenticates endpoints and encrypts data in transit, providing confidentiality and integrity for protocols such as HTTPS.
examples: Configure TLS certificates before serving HTTPS traffic.

sources.title: TLS
sources.snippet: MDN identifies TLS as the protocol used to secure communication over networks.

entries.meaning_short: A distributed network that serves content near users.
entries.meaning_long: A CDN caches and delivers static or dynamic content from geographically distributed nodes to reduce latency and origin load.
examples: Serve asset bundles through a CDN with long cache headers.

sources.title: CDN
sources.snippet: MDN defines CDN as a geographically distributed group of servers for content delivery.

entries.meaning_short: The four basic data operations for persistent resources.
entries.meaning_long: CRUD describes the common create, retrieve, modify, and delete lifecycle used by databases, APIs, admin tools, and resource-oriented interfaces.
examples: An admin panel exposes CRUD operations for glossary entries.

sources.title: CRUD
sources.snippet: MDN expands CRUD as create, read, update, and delete.

entries.meaning_short: Attributes that add accessibility semantics to web UI when native HTML is insufficient.
entries.meaning_long: ARIA roles, states, and properties communicate UI purpose and state to assistive technologies, especially for custom interactive components.
examples: Use aria-expanded on a disclosure button.

sources.title: ARIA
sources.snippet: MDN describes ARIA as attributes for accessible web content and applications.

entries.meaning_short: A common numeronym for Kubernetes.
entries.meaning_long: K8s abbreviates Kubernetes, the container orchestration system used to manage workloads, services, configuration, and cluster resources.
examples: Deploy the service to the K8s cluster.

sources.title: Kubernetes Glossary
sources.snippet: The Kubernetes glossary standardizes Kubernetes terminology.

entries.meaning_short: A Kubernetes API extension that defines a custom resource type.
entries.meaning_long: A CRD registers a new Kubernetes resource schema so operators and controllers can manage domain-specific objects through the Kubernetes API.
examples: Install the operator CRDs before applying custom resources.

sources.title: Kubernetes Glossary
sources.snippet: The Kubernetes glossary includes CustomResourceDefinition terminology.

entries.meaning_short: A plugin specification used to configure container networking.
entries.meaning_long: CNI integrations provide Kubernetes clusters with pod networking behavior such as IP assignment, routing, and network policy support.
examples: Install a CNI plugin before scheduling application pods.

sources.title: Kubernetes Glossary
sources.snippet: The Kubernetes glossary references container networking terminology.

entries.meaning_short: A standard interface for exposing storage systems to container orchestration platforms.
entries.meaning_long: CSI drivers let Kubernetes provision, attach, mount, and manage external storage through a common plugin model.
examples: Install a CSI driver to provision cloud block volumes.

sources.title: Kubernetes Glossary
sources.snippet: The Kubernetes glossary covers storage interface terminology used by clusters.

entries.meaning_short: An access-control model based on roles and bindings.
entries.meaning_long: RBAC grants permissions by assigning subjects to roles that describe allowed operations over resources.
examples: Create an RBAC RoleBinding for a namespace-scoped service account.

sources.title: Kubernetes Glossary
sources.snippet: The Kubernetes glossary includes role-based access control terminology.

entries.meaning_short: A Kubernetes request for persistent storage.
entries.meaning_long: A PVC lets a workload request storage with specific size, access mode, and storage class requirements without binding directly to a storage backend.
examples: Mount a PVC into a database pod.

sources.title: Kubernetes Glossary
sources.snippet: The Kubernetes glossary lists PersistentVolumeClaim terminology.

entries.meaning_short: A Kubernetes storage resource representing provisioned persistent storage.
entries.meaning_long: A PV abstracts storage capacity and access details so pods can consume durable storage through PVCs.
examples: Bind a PV to a PVC for durable application data.

sources.title: Kubernetes Glossary
sources.snippet: The Kubernetes glossary lists PersistentVolume terminology.

entries.meaning_short: A Kubernetes controller that changes replica counts based on metrics.
entries.meaning_long: HPA scales a workload horizontally by increasing or decreasing pod replicas according to observed metrics and target thresholds.
examples: Configure HPA to scale a deployment on CPU utilization.

sources.title: Kubernetes Glossary
sources.snippet: The Kubernetes glossary includes HorizontalPodAutoscaler terminology.

entries.meaning_short: A Kubernetes autoscaling component that adjusts pod resource requests.
entries.meaning_long: VPA recommends or applies CPU and memory request changes for pods so workloads better match observed usage.
examples: Use VPA recommendations to tune memory requests.

sources.title: Kubernetes Glossary
sources.snippet: The Kubernetes glossary includes autoscaling terminology relevant to pods.

entries.meaning_short: A Kubernetes component that adjusts cluster node count for schedulable capacity.
entries.meaning_long: Cluster Autoscaler adds or removes Kubernetes nodes when pending pods need capacity or existing nodes are underused.
examples: On Kubernetes docs pages, CAP should resolve to Cluster Autoscaler before CAP theorem.

sources.title: Node Autoscaling
sources.snippet: Kubernetes documents Cluster Autoscaler as a node autoscaling component.

entries.meaning_short: A Kubernetes classification that affects pod scheduling and eviction behavior.
entries.meaning_long: Kubernetes assigns QoS classes from resource requests and limits, influencing how pods are handled under node resource pressure.
examples: A Guaranteed QoS pod sets equal CPU and memory requests and limits.

sources.title: Kubernetes Glossary
sources.snippet: The Kubernetes glossary includes Quality of Service classes.

entries.meaning_short: A distributed key-value store used by Kubernetes for cluster state.
entries.meaning_long: etcd stores Kubernetes API state and metadata consistently across control-plane members.
examples: Back up etcd before upgrading a Kubernetes control plane.

sources.title: Kubernetes Glossary
sources.snippet: The Kubernetes glossary includes etcd as a control-plane storage component.

entries.meaning_short: The smallest deployable compute unit in Kubernetes.
entries.meaning_long: A pod groups one or more containers with shared networking and storage context for scheduling and lifecycle management.
examples: A deployment creates pods from its pod template.

sources.title: Kubernetes Glossary
sources.snippet: The Kubernetes glossary defines Pod as the smallest deployable unit.

entries.meaning_short: A development practice that frequently integrates changes with automated checks.
entries.meaning_long: CI systems run builds, tests, and other verification when developers push changes so integration problems surface quickly.
examples: CI runs lint, typecheck, and tests for every pull request.

sources.title: Continuous integration
sources.snippet: Wikipedia describes continuous integration as frequent integration with automated verification.

entries.meaning_short: A release practice where software stays deployable through automated build and test stages.
entries.meaning_long: Continuous delivery keeps changes ready for production release, often requiring an explicit approval before deployment.
examples: A CD pipeline prepares a signed artifact for manual production promotion.

sources.title: Continuous delivery
sources.snippet: Wikipedia describes continuous delivery as producing software ready for release.

entries.meaning_short: A release practice that automatically deploys validated changes to production.
entries.meaning_long: Continuous deployment extends delivery by automatically releasing every change that passes the required automated gates.
examples: A successful main-branch build deploys automatically under continuous deployment.

sources.title: Continuous deployment
sources.snippet: Wikipedia distinguishes continuous deployment as automatic production release after validation.

entries.meaning_short: Managing infrastructure through versioned machine-readable definitions.
entries.meaning_long: IaC uses declarative or procedural configuration files to provision and change infrastructure repeatably through tooling and review workflows.
examples: Use Terraform modules as IaC for cloud networking.

sources.title: Infrastructure as code
sources.snippet: Wikipedia describes infrastructure as code as managing infrastructure using machine-readable files.

entries.meaning_short: An engineering discipline for operating reliable services with software methods.
entries.meaning_long: SRE applies engineering practices to service reliability, including observability, incident response, error budgets, and automation.
examples: SRE teams define SLOs and error budgets for critical APIs.

sources.title: Site reliability engineering
sources.snippet: Wikipedia describes SRE as applying software engineering to operations problems.

entries.meaning_short: A contractual commitment about service performance or availability.
entries.meaning_long: An SLA defines agreed service expectations, measurements, and remedies between a provider and customer.
examples: The paid plan includes a 99.9 percent uptime SLA.

sources.title: Service-level agreement
sources.snippet: Wikipedia defines service-level agreement as a service contract commitment.

entries.meaning_short: A target reliability threshold for a service indicator.
entries.meaning_long: An SLO sets an internal or external target for an SLI, such as latency, availability, freshness, or correctness over a defined window.
examples: Set an SLO that 99 percent of search requests complete under 500 ms.

sources.title: Site reliability engineering
sources.snippet: Wikipedia's SRE article discusses service-level objectives in reliability practice.

entries.meaning_short: A metric used to measure service behavior against an objective.
entries.meaning_long: An SLI is the observed measurement, such as request success rate or latency, that an SLO evaluates over time.
examples: Use successful requests divided by total requests as an availability SLI.

sources.title: Site reliability engineering
sources.snippet: Wikipedia's SRE article discusses service-level indicators in reliability practice.

entries.meaning_short: A distributed systems theorem about tradeoffs under network partitions.
entries.meaning_long: CAP theorem states that when a partition occurs, a distributed data system must trade off consistency and availability.
examples: CAP discussions compare consistency and availability choices during a network split.

sources.title: CAP theorem
sources.snippet: Wikipedia describes CAP theorem as a consistency, availability, and partition tolerance result.

entries.meaning_short: A data format for exchanging emergency and public warning alerts.
entries.meaning_long: Common Alerting Protocol standardizes alert messages so systems can share warnings across tools, channels, and jurisdictions.
examples: An incident system ingests a CAP alert feed during emergency response.

sources.title: Common Alerting Protocol
sources.snippet: Wikipedia describes Common Alerting Protocol as an XML-based alerting data format.

entries.meaning_short: Storage whose value is scoped separately to each thread.
entries.meaning_long: Thread-local storage lets code use a variable-like location where each thread observes its own instance rather than shared process-wide state.
examples: Use TLS for per-thread allocator metadata.

sources.title: Thread-local storage
sources.snippet: Wikipedia describes thread-local storage as static or global memory local to a thread.

entries.meaning_short: A request submitted to a certificate authority to obtain a certificate.
entries.meaning_long: A CSR contains identifying information and a public key, letting a CA issue a signed certificate for TLS or related uses.
examples: Generate a CSR before requesting a TLS certificate from a CA.

sources.title: Certificate signing request
sources.snippet: Wikipedia defines a CSR as a message sent to a certificate authority.

entries.meaning_short: Rendering UI in the browser instead of producing full markup on the server.
entries.meaning_long: Client-side rendering sends JavaScript and data to the browser, where application code constructs or updates the visible interface.
examples: A SPA often uses CSR after loading its JavaScript bundle.

sources.title: Client-side rendering
sources.snippet: Wikipedia describes client-side rendering as generating HTML in the browser.

entries.meaning_short: A tree representation of source code structure.
entries.meaning_long: An AST represents parsed program syntax in a form compilers, linters, formatters, and analysis tools can inspect and transform.
examples: A linter walks the AST to find unsafe patterns.

sources.title: Abstract syntax tree
sources.snippet: Wikipedia describes an abstract syntax tree as a tree representation of source code syntax.

entries.meaning_short: A compiler-internal representation between source code and target output.
entries.meaning_long: An IR gives compilers a stable form for analysis, optimization, and code generation across multiple source languages or targets.
examples: LLVM IR is optimized before machine code generation.

sources.title: Intermediate representation
sources.snippet: Wikipedia describes intermediate representation as a data structure used internally by compilers.

entries.meaning_short: The process for detecting, managing, and recovering from incidents.
entries.meaning_long: Incident response coordinates investigation, containment, communication, remediation, and review when security or reliability incidents occur.
examples: Page the IR lead when the production breach runbook triggers.

sources.title: Incident response
sources.snippet: Wikipedia describes incident response as an organized approach to security incidents.

entries.meaning_short: A community fixture for a change-review process acronym.
entries.meaning_long: Change Advisory Process is included as a low-confidence fixture so the UI can verify that T3 entries stay hidden until the confidence toggle is enabled.
examples: Route the release through CAP before production deployment.

sources.title: Change Advisory Process fixture
sources.snippet: Fixture source for a low-confidence community CAP expansion.

entries.meaning_short: A user-contributed fixture for a proxy acronym expansion.
entries.meaning_long: Cloud Access Proxy is included as a T4 fixture so the UI can verify that user-contributed entries stay hidden until explicitly revealed.
examples: The team routed admin traffic through a CAP before reaching internal services.

sources.title: Cloud Access Proxy fixture
sources.snippet: Fixture source for a user-contributed CAP expansion.

entries.meaning_short: A browser policy mechanism for reducing web content injection risks.
entries.meaning_long: Content Security Policy lets sites restrict where scripts, styles, images, and other resources may load from, helping mitigate attacks such as cross-site scripting.
examples: Set a CSP header that only allows scripts from the application origin.

sources.title: CSP
sources.snippet: MDN describes CSP as a policy used to detect and mitigate attacks such as cross-site scripting.

entries.meaning_short: An XML-based vector image format for two-dimensional graphics.
entries.meaning_long: SVG represents scalable shapes, paths, and text in an XML syntax that can be embedded in HTML, styled with CSS, and manipulated with JavaScript.
examples: Use an inline SVG icon for a toolbar button.

sources.title: SVG
sources.snippet: MDN defines SVG as a 2D vector image format based on XML syntax.

entries.meaning_short: A flexible markup language for structured data documents.
entries.meaning_long: XML lets authors define custom tags for data-description languages and is used by formats and protocols that exchange structured documents.
examples: Parse an XML feed before transforming it into JSON.

sources.title: XML
sources.snippet: MDN describes XML as a generic markup language specified by the W3C.

entries.meaning_short: A browser API family for real-time media and peer-to-peer data.
entries.meaning_long: WebRTC enables web apps to access media devices, establish peer connections, and exchange real-time audio, video, or data between browsers.
examples: Use WebRTC to build an in-browser video call.

sources.title: WebRTC
sources.snippet: MDN describes WebRTC as an API used by video chat, voice calling, and peer-to-peer file sharing web apps.

entries.meaning_short: A web app enhanced to behave more like a platform-specific app.
entries.meaning_long: A PWA is built with web platform technologies while using capabilities such as manifests, service workers, and push APIs to provide installable, app-like behavior.
examples: Add a web app manifest and service worker before shipping a PWA.

sources.title: Progressive web applications
sources.snippet: MDN describes PWAs as applications built with web platform technologies that provide a platform-specific-app-like experience.
